title: Major burns
stem: Resus 1. A 30-year-old woman (about 70 kg) was trapped for around 30 minutes in a burning flat before firefighters carried her out an hour ago. She is drowsy, GCS 13. HR 124, BP 96/58, RR 26, SpO2 97% on a non-rebreather. Manage her initial resuscitation.

phases.title: Prepare
phases.goal: Team, PPE, the difficult airway kit, warmth and burns kit. Monitoring on when she arrives.

phases.title: Primary survey
phases.goal: Examine her yourself, A to E: the airway first.

phases.title: Airway
phases.goal: Inhalation injury: decide, intubate yourself, and set the ventilator.

phases.title: Tests and drugs
phases.goal: The gas that sees carbon monoxide; analgesia and tetanus from the cart.

phases.title: Fluids
phases.goal: Size the burn, calculate the fluid, start it, and measure the urine.

phases.title: Burn care and referral
phases.goal: Cover, elevate, watch the limb; burns centre; hand over.

review.text: Dressings for a large burn. Your notes say sterile moist dressings. That suits a small burn, but for a large one (this patient has 36%) cover with clean dry sheets or cling film laid in strips: big wet dressings make the patient hypothermic. First-aid cooling (running water for 20 minutes, within 3 hours) is still right.

Referral criteria. Your notes use the older list (3rd degree over 5%, 20% combined, 10% in the young and old). Current ABA and UK criteria: any full-thickness burn; partial thickness over 10% in adults or 5% in children; face, hands, feet, genitals, perineum or major joints; circumferential burns; inhalation injury; electrical and chemical burns; burns with trauma or significant illness.

Your department's burn unit and burn facility criteria leave out four groups that ABA 2022 and EMSB include: burns with major trauma, suspected non-accidental injury, pregnancy, and every inhalation injury (not only those needing ICU).

The name of the fluid formula. The original Parkland formula is 4 mL/kg/%TBSA; the 2 mL/kg/% starting rate is the ATLS (10th and 11th edition) version. In the exam say 'ATLS 2 mL/kg per % burn', half in the first 8 hours from the time of the burn.

notes:
Checked against ATLS 11th edition, the British Burn Association / NHS burns referral guidance, ABA guidelines (2022 referral criteria) and current UK and HK practice for inhalation injury and carbon monoxide.

Inhalation injury: enclosed space, reduced consciousness, facial burns, singed nasal hair, soot in the mouth or sputum, hoarseness or stridor, and a raised carboxyhaemoglobin. Intubate early with an uncut tube (at least 7.5 in an adult) by the most experienced operator; swelling peaks over 24–48 hours. Suxamethonium is safe in the first 24 hours.

Pulse oximetry reads carboxyhaemoglobin as oxyhaemoglobin: SpO2 is falsely normal. Give 100% oxygen and measure COHb on a co-oximeter gas. Suspect cyanide (lactate over 8 mmol/L, shock, arrest) in enclosed-space fires: hydroxocobalamin 5 g IV.

Burn size counts partial- and full-thickness burns only (not erythema): rule of nines in adults, Lund–Browder in children, the patient's palm and fingers ≈ 1% for scattered burns. Formal fluids for over 20% TBSA in adults (over 10% in children) — ATLS, and your department's burn-unit threshold. UK/NICE practice starts at 15% in adults.

Fluids: ATLS 10th/11th uses 2 mL/kg/%TBSA of Hartmann's for adults (3 mL for children, 4 mL for electrical injury), half in the first 8 hours from the time of the burn, not arrival. Titrate to urine output 0.5 mL/kg/h (1 mL/kg/h in children). The station scores 2 mL/kg/%TBSA only; 4 mL is marked wrong. Naming: the original Parkland formula is 4 mL/kg/%; the 2 mL starting rate is ATLS 10th's modified version (the 'modified Parkland' / Brooke range), so say 'ATLS 2 mL/kg/%' in the exam. The formula is a starting point: over-resuscitation ('fluid creep') causes compartment syndromes.

Dressings: your notes say sterile moist dressings. That is fine for a small burn, and first-aid cooling (running water for 20 minutes within 3 hours) is correct. For a large burn like this one (36%), ATLS says cover with clean, dry, warm sheets or cling film: large wet dressings cool the patient fast, and hypothermia worsens coagulopathy and mortality. Cling film is also non-adherent, eases pain, and lets the burns team see the wound without taking a dressing off. Lay it in strips; don't wrap it round a limb.

Your department's criteria (Burn Unit: over 20% adults / 10% children under 12, inhalation needing ICU, major functional or cosmetic, comorbidity; Burn Facility: extremes of age, over 5%, special areas, comorbidity, chemical, circumferential, electrical, full thickness) broadly match international guidance. Missing compared with ABA 2022 / EMSB: burns with major trauma, suspected non-accidental injury, pregnancy, and all inhalation injury (not only ICU cases). This patient meets the Burn Unit criteria.

Referral: your notes list the older criteria (3rd degree over 5%, 20% combined, 10% in the young and old). Current ABA and UK guidance refer any full-thickness burn, partial-thickness over 10% (adults) or 5% (children), burns of the face, hands, feet, genitals, perineum or major joints, circumferential burns, inhalation injury, electrical and chemical burns, and burns with trauma or significant comorbidity.

Perfect script checked against an ATLS/EMSB checklist, a UK burns-referral checklist, an HKCEM-style scheme and a keyword scheme. Removed every wrong option (wet towels, waiting on the airway, wrong sizes and formulas, wrong doses, antibiotics, steroids, tight wrapping, debriding blisters, a ward admission, a thin handover). Added: the formula said aloud with the time of the burn, suxamethonium stated as safe, breathing, circulation, D and two handover questions now scored.

steps.label: Get the bay ready
steps.hint: Trauma/burns call, PPE, difficult airway kit with uncut tubes, warm room, cling film.

opts.t: Trauma team and anaesthetist now
opts.mark: Calls the trauma team and anaesthetist early

opts.t: PPE
opts.mark: Team in PPE

opts.t: Difficult airway trolley with uncut size 7.5 and 8.0 tubes
opts.mark: Prepares for a difficult airway with uncut tubes

opts.t: Warm the room, warm fluids, warm blankets
opts.mark: Prevents hypothermia

opts.t: Cling film and burns chart
opts.mark: Cling film and a burns chart ready

steps.label: Monitoring
steps.hint: Ask the nurse to put the patient on the monitor.

opts.t: Monitoring on, please: ECG, blood pressure and SpO2, keeping her on 100% oxygen.
opts.mark: Asks for continuous ECG, NIBP and SpO2 monitoring

steps.label: Handover
steps.hint: Enclosed space? Time of the burn? Loss of consciousness? What was given?

Fire.t: Where was she, and for how long?
Fire.r: Trapped in a smoke-filled bedroom, door shut, about 30 minutes.
Fire.mark: Asks about an enclosed space and duration

Fire.r: Fire started about 19:05. We got her out at 19:35. Now 20:05.
Fire.mark: Establishes the time of the burn

Fire.r: Unresponsive when we found her, woke up in the ambulance.

Treatment.r: Oxygen by mask. Nothing else. No cooling — too big an area.

Treatment.t: Any other injury, falls or explosion?

steps.label: Primary survey
steps.hint: Airway signs of inhalation, breathing, circulation, D, then expose and map the burn.

Airway.t: Look at the face, nose and mouth
Airway.r: Facial erythema, singed nasal hair and eyebrows, soot on the tongue and palate. "Signs of inhalation injury."
Airway.mark: Finds signs of inhalation injury (singed hair, soot)

Airway.t: Listen to her voice and breathing
Airway.r: Hoarse voice. Soft inspiratory stridor now. "The airway is going to swell shut."
Airway.mark: Recognises hoarseness and stridor as airway threat

Breathing.r: Partial-thickness burns on the chest, not circumferential. Scattered wheeze. RR 26.
Breathing.mark: Assesses breathing: chest burns not circumferential

Circulation.r: Two 16 G cannulae through unburnt skin in the left forearm and right foot.
Circulation.mark: IV access, through unburnt skin if possible

D E.r: GCS 13 (E3 V4 M6). Pupils equal. Glucose 6.2.

D E.t: Expose fully and map the burns
D E.r: Face red only. Chest, abdomen and left arm: blistered, pink, painful (partial thickness). Right arm: white, leathery, painless, circumferential (full thickness).
D E.mark: Maps burn depth and extent on a chart

D E.r: Rings and watch off before the hands swell.

steps.label: The airway
steps.hint: Stridor and hoarseness with soot: intubate early, uncut tube, most experienced operator.

opts.t: She has an inhalation injury with stridor: intubate now, before the swelling, with the most experienced operator and an uncut 8.0 tube.
opts.mark: Decides on early intubation with an uncut tube
opts.r: Anaesthetist: Agreed. I'll take the airway with you; videolaryngoscope ready.

opts.t: Suxamethonium is safe in the first 24 hours after a burn.
opts.mark: Knows suxamethonium is safe in the first 24 hours

Airway.t: Intubate: laryngoscope, tube through the cords, cuff up, capnography
Airway.r: Tube through the cords, cuff up. Capnography: a square trace on every breath.
Airway.mark: Intubates early with an uncut tube

steps.label: Ventilator
steps.hint: Set it yourself: lung-protective, 100% oxygen for the carbon monoxide.

opts.t: Set the ventilator
opts.performHint: Intubated, 70 kg. A controlled mode, 6–8 mL/kg, normocapnia, FiO2 100% for the CO. START.

steps.label: Investigations
steps.hint: A co-oximetry gas (COHb, lactate), ECG, chest film, bloods and group.

Gas.t: Arterial or venous gas with co-oximetry
Gas.r: COHb 22%. Lactate 5.8. pH 7.29. PaO2 on oxygen 38 kPa. "The SpO2 was falsely normal."

Other.t: FBC, U&E, CK, group and save, pregnancy test
Other.mark: Baseline bloods including CK and pregnancy test

steps.label: Drug cart
steps.hint: Analgesia, tetanus; hydroxocobalamin if cyanide is likely.

opts.t: Morphine 2–5 mg IV, titrated to pain
opts.mark: IV analgesia titrated

opts.t: Tetanus vaccine (Td/IPV) 0.5 mL IM
opts.mark: Tetanus prophylaxis

opts.t: Hydroxocobalamin 5 g IV over 15 minutes
opts.mark: Considers cyanide: hydroxocobalamin

steps.label: Fluid plan
steps.hint: Burn size and the fluid formula.

opts.t: Burn size by the rule of nines: chest 9, abdomen 9, both arms 18: 36% TBSA. The red face is erythema, which doesn't count.
opts.mark: Calculates TBSA without counting erythema

opts.t: ATLS formula: 2 mL per kg per % burn: 2 × 70 × 36 = 5040 mL of Hartmann's in 24 hours. Half, 2520 mL, in the first 8 hours from the time of the burn at 19:05; she's an hour in, so 360 mL an hour.
opts.mark: Uses 2 mL/kg/%TBSA, half in 8 hours from the time of the burn

steps.label: Drug cart
steps.hint: Start the burn fluid at the rate you calculated.

opts.t: Hartmann's 360 mL/h (2520 mL by 8 hours after the burn)
opts.dose: 360 mL/h (2520 mL by 8 hours after the burn)
opts.mark: Calculates fluids and times them from the burn

opts.t: Urinary catheter; urine output 0.5 mL/kg/h (35 mL/h) and titrate the fluid to it
opts.mark: Catheter and urine output target

steps.label: Burn care
steps.hint: Cling film in strips, keep warm, elevate, watch the circumferential arm.

opts.t: Cling film laid in strips, not wrapped round the limbs
opts.mark: Covers with cling film laid in strips

opts.t: Elevate the burnt limbs
opts.mark: Elevates burnt limbs

opts.t: Check pulses in the right hand hourly: circumferential full-thickness burn
opts.mark: Monitors the circumferential burn for escharotomy

steps.label: Phone
steps.hint: Refer to the burns centre: size, full thickness, circumferential, inhalation.

opts.t: Burns centre: a 30-year-old woman, 36% TBSA with a full-thickness circumferential right arm, inhalation injury, intubated, COHb 22%. She needs your unit.
opts.mark: Refers to the burns centre with the key criteria
opts.r: Burns consultant: Accept. Transfer when stable; call if the arm needs escharotomy first.

steps.ask: The burns team has arrived. Please hand over.
steps.label: Handover
steps.hint: SBAR with times, TBSA, fluids and airway.

opts.t: Handover in SBAR: Ms Chow, 30, burnt at 19:05 in an enclosed space. Inhalation injury: intubated, COHb 22%, on 100% oxygen; hydroxocobalamin given. 36% TBSA, full-thickness circumferential right arm: pulses checked hourly. Hartmann's at 360 mL/h, urine target 35 mL/h. Burns centre has accepted.
opts.mark: Structured handover with times, TBSA, fluids and plan
opts.r: The retrieval team repeat it back.

qs.q: Which finding does NOT suggest inhalation injury?
wrong: Soot in the mouth and nose
The probe sits on a burnt, poorly perfused finger
Smoke particles in the blood scatter the light
CO shifts the curve to the right

qs.q: Which burns count toward TBSA for fluids?
wrong: Full thickness only, as partial heals
Any burn larger than 1% on its own

qs.q: Best way to estimate burn size in a child?
qs.why: Children's heads are proportionally larger and legs smaller than the adult rule of nines.

qs.q: Urine output target in an adult with burns?

rules.fail: Fluids or dressings before the airway.

badge.name: Fire Walker
badge.flavor: Tube early and uncut. Count from the burn, not the door.

cards.why: Half in the first 8 hours from the burn, the rest over 16; titrate to urine output.
cards.note: Original Parkland uses 4 mL; ATLS 10th starts adults at 2 mL.

cards.q: The first 8 hours of burn fluids are timed from…
cards.why: Any delay must be caught up.

cards.q: Carbon monoxide poisoning: SpO2 on a standard oximeter is…
cards.why: COHb absorbs light like oxyhaemoglobin at the oximeter's wavelengths. Use co-oximetry.

cards.q: Antidote for cyanide from smoke inhalation?
cards.why: It binds cyanide to form cyanocobalamin, excreted in urine.

cards.q: How should cling film be applied to a burnt arm?
options: Laid in strips along the limb
cards.why: Wrapping acts as a tourniquet as the limb swells.

cards.q: Urine output target in a child with major burns?
Which is NOT a burns centre referral criterion?
options: Circumferential full-thickness burn of the forearm
cards.why: Erythema is not counted and a small superficial burn is managed locally.
cards.source: ABA 2022; UK National Burn Care Referral Guidance

script.say: Trauma team and the anaesthetist now, please. Team in PPE. Difficult airway trolley with uncut 7.5 and 8.0 tubes. Warm the room, warm fluids and blankets. Cling film and a burns chart.
Monitoring on, please: ECG, blood pressure and SpO2, keeping her on 100% oxygen.
Where was she, and for how long? What time was the burn? Was she unconscious? What has been done? Any fall or explosion?
script.do: Enclosed smoke-filled bedroom for 30 minutes; fire at 19:05; unresponsive at first; oxygen only; no other trauma.

script.say: Airway: singed nasal hair and eyebrows, soot on the tongue, a hoarse voice and soft stridor: an inhalation injury; the airway is going to swell shut.
Breathing: RR 26, scattered wheeze, chest burns not circumferential. Circulation: HR 124, BP 96/58, refill 3 seconds; two large cannulae through unburnt skin. GCS 13, pupils equal, glucose 6.2.
Exposure: chest, abdomen and left arm blistered and painful: partial thickness. Right arm white, leathery and painless, all the way round: full thickness, circumferential. Rings and watch off.
She has an inhalation injury with stridor: intubate now, before the swelling, with the most experienced operator and an uncut 8.0 tube. Suxamethonium is safe in the first 24 hours after a burn.
Ventilator: volume control, 6 to 8 mL per kg, a rate for normocapnia, FiO2 100% for the carbon monoxide.
A gas with co-oximetry for carboxyhaemoglobin: the SpO2 is falsely normal with carbon monoxide. 12-lead ECG, chest X-ray; FBC, U&E, CK, group and save, and a pregnancy test.
Shocked with a lactate of 5.8 after an enclosed-space fire: possible cyanide: hydroxocobalamin 5 g IV over 15 minutes. Morphine 2 to 5 mg IV titrated to pain. Tetanus vaccine.
Burn size by the rule of nines: chest 9, abdomen 9, both arms 18: 36% TBSA. The red face is erythema, which doesn't count.

ATLS formula: 2 mL per kg per % burn: 2 × 70 × 36 = 5040 mL of Hartmann's in 24 hours. Half, 2520 mL, in the first 8 hours from the time of the burn at 19:05; she's an hour in, so 360 mL an hour. Urinary catheter: urine output 0.5 mL per kg per hour, 35 mL an hour, and titrate to it.
Cling film laid in strips, not wrapped round the limbs. Elevate the burnt limbs. Check the pulses in the right hand hourly: a circumferential full-thickness burn may need escharotomy.
Burns centre: a 30-year-old woman, 36% TBSA with a full-thickness circumferential right arm, inhalation injury, intubated, COHb 22%. She needs your unit.

Handover in SBAR: Ms Chow, 30, burnt at 19:05 in an enclosed space. Inhalation injury: intubated, COHb 22%, on 100% oxygen; hydroxocobalamin given. 36% TBSA, full-thickness circumferential right arm: pulses checked hourly. Hartmann's at 360 mL/h, urine target 35 mL/h. Burns centre has accepted.
